description: Gözlemsel astronomi, robotik sistem geliştirme ve yazılım prototipleme alanlarındaki çalışmalarımı disiplinler arası bir yaklaşımla birleştirerek NASA Space Apps Challenge için yenilikçi ve çözüm odaklı bir ekip oluşturuyorum. Bilimi ve teknolojiyi yalnızca teorik bir düzeyde ele almak yerine, gerçek dünya problemlerine somut çözümler üretebilen, merak ve araştırma tutkusuyla hareket eden üyeleri bir araya getiriyoruz.
summary:
ADEX is a web-based science communication tool that turns NASA SPHEREx infrared data into an interactive experience for students, educators and amateur astronomers. It has two separate modules. In “Scan”, users compare two observations of the same sky area using blink, side-by-side and difference views. They mark a changing source and save it as a candidate card, with coordinates and a clear data-origin label. In “Lab”, users adjust the parameters of a clearly simulated exoplanet, such as albedo, orbital distance, stellar luminosity, greenhouse factor, ocean fraction and surface pressure. They see the effect on surface temperature using a simple energy-balance model.

SPHEREx maps the whole sky in near-infrared but does not detect or confirm exoplanets on its own. ADEX therefore never claims a discovery. It only reports “changing-source candidates” that need independent verification. Every value carries a label (OBSERVED, CATALOG-MATCHED, ESTIMATED, USER-SIMULATED or ILLUSTRATIVE), so real observations and model assumptions are never mixed. ADEX makes complex survey data accessible while keeping the science honest.
details:
ADEX guides the user through three steps: Scan, Lab, Report.

  1. Scan. The user loads two epochs of a real NASA SPHEREx infrared image (Epoch A and Epoch B) and compares them. Blink, side-by-side and difference modes make changes visible. Clicking a position creates a candidate card with its pixel coordinates. The card can be sent to the Lab or exported as JSON. A SPHEREx FITS analysis pipeline produces a JSON spectrum file. The app loads it and plots the measured spectrum for the selected sky position, labeled OBSERVED. The card states that this is not an exoplanet discovery and that independent verification is required.
  2. Lab. This module is separate from the NASA observation and is labeled as a simulated exoplanet with hypothetical parameters. The user can pick a preset (rocky–temperate, ice, hot, rocky–thin atmosphere) or change nine parameters: albedo, orbital distance, stellar luminosity, greenhouse factor, ocean fraction, surface pressure, mass, radius and magnetic shield. A reference planet and a scenario planet are shown side by side with the temperature change. The model uses a one-layer global-mean energy balance, T_eq = [S(1 − A) / 4σ]^(1/4), and an educational greenhouse factor to estimate surface temperature. It also derives surface gravity, escape velocity, boiling point and a radiation index. A habitability index (0–100) is shown as an educational indicator, and a temperature-versus-distance chart marks the temperate zone.
  3. Report. The finding or scenario can be exported with its sources, labels and model version.

The app also lets users write their own scenario in text and save it, and it supports a language selector (Turkish in our screenshots).

Real observations and context

A reference section sets real data next to illustrations and names each type: a real SPHEREx image of the Cygnus X region (ice and PAH emission), NASA’s artist concept of TRAPPIST-1, and a real Webb NIRSpec spectrum of WASP-39 b showing CO₂. Users can see what is a measurement, a model or an illustration.

Scientific integrity

SPHEREx maps the sky in 102 spectral bands (about 0.75–5 µm). Moving or changing sources can be asteroids, variable stars, alignment errors or processing artifacts, so ADEX treats a marked point only as a candidate. We avoid phrases such as “new exoplanet discovered” and use “changing-source candidate” and “catalog match pending”. Our five data labels follow every value through the interface, and a value the user edits is never shown as OBSERVED. The Lab states that the model does not solve clouds, ocean circulation or atmospheric chemistry, and the planet images are representative.

Benefits and intended impact

ADEX makes a large, complex survey easier to approach for non-experts. It also teaches the difference between observation, estimation and assumption, and links infrared astronomy to planetary climate and habitability concepts. We aim to help students and educators explore real NASA data, build scientific literacy, and see why verification matters.

Tools and technologies — please check this against what you actually built before pasting:

  • Front end: single-page web app (HTML/CSS/JavaScript) with a dark mission-control style interface, an image canvas for blink/side-by-side/difference views, and interactive charts [fill in framework, e.g. React/Vite].
  • Data: NASA SPHEREx images (IRSA/IPAC), a FITS-based analysis step that outputs JSON spectra [fill in Python libraries, e.g. Astropy/NumPy], and NASA/JPL mission pages for context.
  • Model: one-layer energy-balance equations in JavaScript [or Python/NumPy], with unit and range checks.
  • Hosting: [fill in, e.g. Vercel/Netlify/GitHub Pages].
  • Data sources: NASA SPHEREx / IRSA, NASA Exoplanet Archive, NASA/JPL, NASA Webb.

Creativity

Most tools show either data or simulation. ADEX puts both in one journey but keeps them strictly separated by labels, by module and by interface wording, so the user always knows what is real. We also designed the language itself as part of the product. “Candidate” replaces “discovery”, and every card includes its own limitation statement.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific limits: SPHEREx is not an exoplanet-detection mission, and the climate model is educational only.
  • Accessibility: color never carries meaning alone, so labels are also written as text. The layout is readable, and the interface offers multiple languages.
  • Data availability: the app shows an explicit data-origin label so users can tell real and demo data apart.
  • Scope: we prioritized comparing real images, marking changes, source cards and a basic climate model over automatic detection or full climate simulation.
  • Future work: in-app IRSA queries, WCS-based alignment and photometry, catalog cross-matching, NASA Exoplanet Archive integration, advanced climate models reviewed by experts, and a teacher mode.
